items.title: Anthropic Releases Claude Opus 5 at Half the Token Price of Claude Fable 5
items.summary: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5 , offering token pricing at half the rate of Claude Fable 5 and claiming near-frontier performance, according to Anthropic and The Register. Opus 5 is priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50 for Fable 5. Anthropic states the model "comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price." Opus 5 does not require data retention. Anthropic describes Opus 5 as its "most aligned model to date." The company reports it outperforms Opus 4.8 overall, with the greatest improvements in agentic coding, computer use, and long-horizon knowledge work. Pricing and Benchmark Position, Shorter System Prompt and Changed Context Guidance Fable 5 is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, while Opus 5 is $5 and $25. For comparison, The Register notes that OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol costs $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens. Since token usage per task varies by model, per-task cost is a distinct metric. Artificial Analysis reports the weighted average cost per Intelligence Index task as $2.75 for Fable, $2.03 for Opus 5 at maximum settings, $1.04 for GPT-5.6 Sol at maximum settings, and $0.95 for Kimi K3. Opus 5 leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 61, one point ahead of Fable. Anthropic claims Opus 5 "provides greatly improved performance for the same cost as its predecessor, Opus 4.8." The system card states it is comparable to, and in some cases surpasses, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5. Anthropic has reduced the system prompt size in its latest models. Claude Code engineer Thariq Shihipar states that 80 percent of the Claude Code system prompt was removed, allowing customers more context to use. Consequently, Anthropic has updated its guidance for crafting prompts, skills, and CLAUDE.md files. "Across your system prompt, skills, and CLAUDE.md files, you may need to simplify just like we did," Shihipar said, noting that a command called claude doctor can automatically optimize some prompts and skills. The Register notes that Opus 5 responses may run longer than prior Opus models. Anthropic cautions that "Claude Opus 5's default user-facing responses run longer than prior Opus models'" and advises customers to "prompt for it explicitly" to control response length, since longer responses increase output token costs. Cybersecurity, What Opus 5 Means for API Users, And Availability Opus 5 scores close to Mythos on finding vulnerabilities in open source code, with an 80 percent OSS-Fuzz benchmark score compared to 79.4 percent for Mythos. It is significantly weaker at weaponizing those findings, succeeding in 4 of 14 exploitation attempts compared to 13 of 14 for Mythos. Anthropic states that Opus 5's cyber classifiers are proportionally less restrictive than those on Fable 5. According to Anthropic, they "allow Opus 5 to find vulnerabilities in source code, but block 'binary-based' vulnerability scanning (a method more likely to be associated with malicious actors), penetration testing, and exploit generation." The Register notes the model is likely to be more useful for cybersecurity and biology tasks because it refuses to cooperate less often than some other models. Anthropic is also rolling out an automated fallback function on its API. Requests deemed too dangerous to route to Opus 5 or Fable 5 can be sent to a less capable model instead of being blocked outright. For developers and enterprises using Anthropic's API, the practical points to assess are: Compare per-task cost rather than only per-token pricing, since Opus 5 at maximum settings costs $2.03 per Intelligence Index task versus $2.75 for Fable, but GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 remain lower on that measure. Budget for the noted response verbosity by prompting explicitly for shorter responses where output token cost matters, since Opus 5 defaults to longer replies. Review and simplify existing system prompts, skills, and CLAUDE.md files, and run claude doctor to optimize prompts and skills for the new models. Evaluate the automated API fallback function if refusals have previously blocked workflows, since it reroutbes rather than blocks flagged requests. Confirm the data retention terms, since Opus 5 does not carry the data retention requirement applied to some covered models. Anthropic released Opus 5 on Friday, July 24, 2026. The lack of a data retention requirement is likely to be a significant point for businesses, according to The Register. Anthropic has not detailed how the automated fallback routing selects the less capable target model, or published the full list of task categories affected by the adjusted cyber classifiers beyond the binary scanning, penetration testing, and exploit generation restrictions it named. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Anthropic Releases Claude Opus 5 at Half the Token Price of Claude Fable 5 appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Facebook Adds Free Video Selfie Verification With a White Check Mark Badge
items.summary: Meta is adding a free verification feature called Facebook Verified that lets users earn a white check mark by uploading a selfie video, according to Meta's announcement and reporting from Lifehacker. The badge is intended to indicate a real person behind an account and will appear on profiles and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. Facebook Verified is separate from Meta Verified, the paid subscription that provides a blue check mark. The feature is launching in select markets before a global rollout. Meta says it will store the selfie video for up to 30 days after the one-time verification. Lifehacker raises privacy considerations around providing additional biometric data to Meta. How Facebook Verified Works and Differs From Meta Verified Facebook Verified is available to users aged 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with Facebook's community standards. Once a user has access, they record a short selfie video, which Facebook compares to existing profile photos on the account using facial recognition. If verification is approved, the white check mark is added to the profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. At launch, the badge will not appear on Feed posts, though Facebook says it plans to add that placement in the future. The badge will appear across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups from launch. Facebook Verified is distinct from Meta Verified. Meta Verified is a paid subscription that provides a blue check mark on Facebook and Instagram, and confirms a user's identity based on a review of a government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. Facebook Verified, by contrast, is free and relies on a selfie video compared against existing profile photos rather than a government ID review. The white check mark functions as a trust signal to other users rather than a paid identity confirmation. Privacy Considerations Before You Verify Meta states it will store the selfie video for up to 30 days after verification, which is a one-time process. Lifehacker notes it is not entirely clear how the video is handled during that retention window, and points out that Meta has previously used user data to train its AI systems. Lifehacker advises users to weigh whether the verification badge is worth providing additional biometric data to Meta, and to read the privacy policy before agreeing to the process. Facial recognition data is biometric data, and the selfie video is subject to Meta's retention and data-handling practices during the stated 30-day window. Users considering Facebook Verified should assess the tradeoff before recording a selfie video: Confirm eligibility, since the feature requires an account in good standing, a user aged 18 or older, and availability in the user's market at launch. Read Meta's privacy policy covering the selfie video, focusing on the up to 30-day retention window and how the video may be used during that period. Review existing Meta AI data permissions on the account, since Meta has used user data for AI training in the past. Decide whether the white check mark's value as a trust signal outweighs providing biometric facial recognition data. Verify the badge placement matters for the intended use, since it appears in Marketplace, Dating, and Groups but not yet in Feed posts. Google’s Selfie Verification Lands the Same Week Lifehacker notes that Google launched its own video selfie verification feature this week, though it serves a different purpose. Google's feature is designed to prove identity for account recovery when a user is locked out, and it grants access to the entire Google account. Facebook Verified, by contrast, is a trust signal displayed to other users rather than an account recovery mechanism. Because Google's selfie verification can unlock full account access, Lifehacker notes it carries additional security considerations distinct from Facebook's profile badge. Facebook Verified is rolling out in select markets initially, with a global rollout planned but not dated. Facebook has not confirmed which markets receive the feature first, when Feed post badges will be added, or when the feature will expand to additional account types. Meta has not detailed what happens to the stored selfie video at the end of the 30-day retention period beyond stating that storage lasts up to 30 days. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Facebook Adds Free Video Selfie Verification With a White Check Mark Badge appeared first on gHacks .

How Facebook Verified Works and Differs From Meta Verified

Once a user has access, they record a short selfie video, which Facebook compares to existing profile photos on the account using facial recognition. If verification is approved, the white check mark is added to the profile.

Facebook Verified, by contrast, is free and relies on a selfie video compared against existing profile photos rather than a government ID review. The white check mark functions as a trust signal to other users rather than a paid identity confirmation.

Meta states it will store the selfie video for up to 30 days after verification, which is a one-time process. Lifehacker notes it is not entirely clear how the video is handled during that retention window, and points out that Meta has previously used user data to train its AI systems.

Facial recognition data is biometric data, and the selfie video is subject to Meta's retention and data-handling practices during the stated 30-day window.

Users considering Facebook Verified should assess the tradeoff before recording a selfie video:

  1. Confirm eligibility, since the feature requires an account in good standing, a user aged 18 or older, and availability in the user's market at launch.
  2. Read Meta's privacy policy covering the selfie video, focusing on the up to 30-day retention window and how the video may be used during that period.
  3. Review existing Meta AI data permissions on the account, since Meta has used user data for AI training in the past.
  4. Decide whether the white check mark's value as a trust signal outweighs providing biometric facial recognition data.
  5. Verify the badge placement matters for the intended use, since it appears in Marketplace, Dating, and Groups but not yet in Feed posts.

Because Google's selfie verification can unlock full account access, Lifehacker notes it carries additional security considerations distinct from Facebook's profile badge.

Facebook Verified is rolling out in select markets initially, with a global rollout planned but not dated. Facebook has not confirmed which markets receive the feature first, when Feed post badges will be added, or when the feature will expand to additional account types.

Meta has not detailed what happens to the stored selfie video at the end of the 30-day retention period beyond stating that storage lasts up to 30 days.

items.title: I help wealthy families get their kids into top colleges. Here are 5 strategies any parents can use.
items.summary: Lindsay Tanne Howe is the founder of LogicPrep, a global college advisory firm. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe Lindsay Tanne Howe started a college advisory firm as a Harvard freshman. The company advises ultrawealthy families on how to get their kids into top colleges. Her tips for parents to boost their kids' chances of success include encouraging curiosity. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lindsay Tanne Howe, 37, who is based in Connecticut. She is the founder and CEO of LogicPrep, a global college advisory firm serving ultra-high-net-worth families. Business Insider has verified her educational background. This piece has been edited for length and clarity. A big misconception about college admissions is that getting into a top school comes down to a single magical turning point. In reality, it works like compound interest, where every small decision builds on the last. Admissions success is built more on how your kids spend their average Tuesday than on any one score, grade, or breakthrough moment. Over the past 19 years, I've shared these kinds of insights with ultrawealthy families and their children, but I think any parent can benefit from the advice we give our clients. Have you worked for a billionaire or the ultrawealthy? Business Insider wants to hear your story. Contact this reporter at jzitser@businessinsider.com . I went from Harvard freshman to college admissions advisor I founded LogicPrep in 2007 while I was a freshman at Harvard. I'd successfully navigated the admissions process myself and, with the hubris of a teenager, thought it was my turn to help others. What started as a summer job has become a global college advisory firm serving ultrawealthy families . Our advisors are all former admissions officers who have evaluated thousands of applications, while our essay coaches are professional writers who help students bring their stories to life on the page. In our work, we don't assume a preordained definition of success. We're not Ivy or bust. It's about helping each child become the most self-actualized, deeply engaged version of themselves. Here are five ways the ultrawealthy parents I work with help make that happen. Lindsay Tanne Howe started advising students on college admissions as a summer job while at Harvard. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe 1. Cr eate habits that build curiosity The children of wealthy parents often travel and overhear conversations about work, giving them natural exposure to experiences that spark questions. For all parents, though, it's important to create the habits and mindsets that cultivate curiosity from an early age. In my family, we do that by listening to podcasts in the car and discussing interesting articles over dinner. We also take our children's interests seriously. If your child expresses an interest, take them to the library, find a relevant book, and follow that thread. 2. All work, not just a 'fancy' internship, is a good opportunity to build skills We see many ultrawealthy families tap into their networks early on to create shadowing opportunities for their children. It's a great way to give kids exposure to different careers. Students, however, shouldn't be discouraged if they don't have access to a "fancy" internship . Colleges take context seriously, and students should not be disadvantaged by a lack of access to higher-level opportunities. All work is good exposure and an opportunity to develop interpersonal skills, resilience, and responsibility. Some of the best college essays I've read have been about caddying on a golf course or waitressing at a restaurant. 3. Plan early One advantage wealthy families have is that they know to seek advice from a qualified advisor early on in the admissions process. But thoughtful, proactive planning, which is a clear advantage in the admissions process, isn't exclusive to those with means. You just have to know when to start. The right time to start planning is the tail end of middle school or early high school. That doesn't mean asking an eighth grader to start SAT prep. It means thinking about the classes they're taking and where those could lead, and encouraging them to try different activities. It can also be as simple as visiting a college campus while you're on a trip to make the college application experience feel more tangible. Lindsay Tanne Howe founded LogicPrep in 2007. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe 4. Help your kids find their voice Wealthy families tend to acknowledge and reward their children's authentic voices. In my experience, they really see them as emerging young adults with something to say. They invite their children into conversations with adults and ask them not just where they want to go to college, but what kind of life they want to build. That helps instil a belief in their voice. As a parent, you want to help your child become the narrator of their own life. Ask questions like, "What's the best thing that happened this week?" or "What's your intention for the summer?" 5. Finally, focus on building an 'interesting life,' not an 'impressive application' I really push back against the instinct to build an impressive application . I encourage students to build a genuinely interesting life. There's no perfect applicant or magic formula for college admissions. Simply encourage your child to pursue what genuinely interests them. Do they like marine biology? Take them to the aquarium and encourage them to apply for volunteer opportunities or internships there. The goal isn't to create the perfect applicant. It's to encourage your child, take them seriously, and to help them become the most genuine, engaged, deeply authentic version of themselves. Read the original article on Business Insider

I went from Harvard freshman to college admissions advisor

I founded LogicPrep in 2007 while I was a freshman at Harvard. I'd successfully navigated the admissions process myself and, with the hubris of a teenager, thought it was my turn to help others.

In our work, we don't assume a preordained definition of success. We're not Ivy or bust. It's about helping each child become the most self-actualized, deeply engaged version of themselves. Here are five ways the ultrawealthy parents I work with help make that happen.

Lindsay Tanne Howe started advising students on college admissions as a summer job while at Harvard.

Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe

1. Create habits that build curiosity

The children of wealthy parents often travel and overhear conversations about work, giving them natural exposure to experiences that spark questions. For all parents, though, it's important to create the habits and mindsets that cultivate curiosity from an early age.

In my family, we do that by listening to podcasts in the car and discussing interesting articles over dinner. We also take our children's interests seriously.

If your child expresses an interest, take them to the library, find a relevant book, and follow that thread.

2. All work, not just a 'fancy' internship, is a good opportunity to build skills

All work is good exposure and an opportunity to develop interpersonal skills, resilience, and responsibility. Some of the best college essays I've read have been about caddying on a golf course or waitressing at a restaurant.

3. Plan early

One advantage wealthy families have is that they know to seek advice from a qualified advisor early on in the admissions process. But thoughtful, proactive planning, which is a clear advantage in the admissions process, isn't exclusive to those with means. You just have to know when to start.

The right time to start planning is the tail end of middle school or early high school. That doesn't mean asking an eighth grader to start SAT prep. It means thinking about the classes they're taking and where those could lead, and encouraging them to try different activities.

It can also be as simple as visiting a college campus while you're on a trip to make the college application experience feel more tangible.

Lindsay Tanne Howe founded LogicPrep in 2007.

Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe

4. Help your kids find their voice

Wealthy families tend to acknowledge and reward their children's authentic voices. In my experience, they really see them as emerging young adults with something to say. They invite their children into conversations with adults and ask them not just where they want to go to college, but what kind of life they want to build. That helps instil a belief in their voice.

As a parent, you want to help your child become the narrator of their own life. Ask questions like, "What's the best thing that happened this week?" or "What's your intention for the summer?"

5. Finally, focus on building an 'interesting life,' not an 'impressive application'

I really push back against the instinct to build an impressive application. I encourage students to build a genuinely interesting life.

There's no perfect applicant or magic formula for college admissions. Simply encourage your child to pursue what genuinely interests them. Do they like marine biology? Take them to the aquarium and encourage them to apply for volunteer opportunities or internships there.

The goal isn't to create the perfect applicant. It's to encourage your child, take them seriously, and to help them become the most genuine, engaged, deeply authentic version of themselves.

items.title: JPMorgan’s AI leadership is getting a reset. These are the key players.
items.summary: JPMorgan's AI leadership has recently been reshuffled. Bloomberg/Getty Images JPMorgan's AI chief announced her retirement earlier this month. Her departure left a void in the bank's AI leadership and reshuffled the top tech ranks. We mapped out who is now leading JPMorgan's AI strategy as it vies to be a tech powerhouse. JPMorgan has some new answers to the multibillion-dollar question of who's in charge of AI at the bank. The firm's AI chief, Teresa Heitsenrether, announced her retirement earlier this month after four decades at the bank, reshuffling the technology leadership. It's more than just job titles shifting around — JPMorgan said it's restructuring its firm-wide chief data and analytics office as it transitions from focusing on AI infrastructure to business initiatives. "With the foundations now in place, and AI delivery shifting more to business and functions, we believe that aligning CDAO with Global Technology will best position us to continue our momentum to deliver for our clients and colleagues," according to a memo seen by Business Insider. JPMorgan also announced in the memo that Gerard Francis, formerly the chief product officer of data and AI, is leaving the firm. In February, the bank's head of AI research, Manuela Veloso, left after eight years. The bank, with its nearly $20 billion technology budget, has been especially bullish on AI. CEO Jamie Dimon said on a recent earnings call that there are already more than 1,000 use cases for AI, and Business Insider previously reported that JPMorgan can track individual engineers' token usage. With Heitsenrether leaving, here's who is directing the bank's AI strategy and rollout as it aims to remain a tech leader on Wall Street. Lori Beer As the global chief information officer, Lori Beer sits at the top of the firm's technology leadership , overseeing all the systems and infrastructure. She's a member of the operating committee and manages the bank's sprawling tech budget and nearly 65,000 technologists. Beer joined JPMorgan in 2014. Scot Baldry Scot Baldry already had a big job as JPMorgan's Chief Technology Officer, and is taking on even more responsibility as the Chief Data and Analytics Officer now that Heitsenrether has announced her retirement. In that role, Baldry will helm the bank's overall AI program and strategy. Baldry joined JPMorgan in London in 2022, after stints at Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse, and T. Rowe Price, and reports to Beer. According to an internal memo announcing his expanded remit, Baldry will continue working with technology leaders across business lines to make sure the firm's AI strategy remains consistent. The memo said his team will "focus on AI & data strategy and governance, commercialization and value delivery, and external engagement with policymakers, regulators and the broader ecosystem." Manoj Sindhwani As part of the recent shakeup, Manoj Sindhwani, who was already the chief information officer for AI/ML and data platforms, is also taking responsibility for the bank's data and AI product team. He now oversees the employees who design and build firmwide data platforms and execute the broad strategy. Sindhwani has been at JPMorgan since 2024, after nearly a decade at Amazon, and reports to Beer. William Patrick Opet William Patrick Opet oversees all of JPMorgan's information security, technology controls, and risk management, which have become increasingly pressing issues in the age of AI. As part of his job, Opet ensures that the bank's AI systems are secure and appropriately controlled, and that the firm is protected against cyber threats, including those enabled by AI. Opet joined JPMorgan in 2014 after working at Lockheed Martin and has been in his current role since 2021. He reports to Beer. Mark Birkhead As the firmwide chief data officer, Mark Birkhead's role has only become more crucial as AI has gotten more advanced. JPMorgan has more than an exabyte , or one billion gigabytes, of data across the firm, and Birkhead is the man who ensures it's AI-ready for both LLMs and generative AI. Birkhead, who joined JPMorgan in 2020 and now reports to Baldry, said in a recent post on LinkedIn that "data strategy is the competitive differentiator in banking." Arvind Joshi Arvind Joshi manages JPMorgan's almost $20 billion annual technology budget , including its investments in AI. He oversees resource allocation and has recently commented on the importance of managing the ballooning price of AI tokens on LinkedIn. Joshi has been at JPMorgan for more than two decades and reports to Beer. Sumitra Ganesh Sumitra Ganesh took over as the head of AI research at JPMorgan in February, the latest position in her decade-long run at the bank. Veloso, who left in February, started the research team in 2018, and told Business Insider in 2021 that it focuses on big, "what-if" questions. As of April, JPMorgan had the largest AI research team among the 50 banks that the intelligence platform Evident AI tracks. Ganesh's research has primarily focused on multi-agent systems in finance, according to her LinkedIn. Read the original article on Business Insider

It's more than just job titles shifting around — JPMorgan said it's restructuring its firm-wide chief data and analytics office as it transitions from focusing on AI infrastructure to business initiatives.

"With the foundations now in place, and AI delivery shifting more to business and functions, we believe that aligning CDAO with Global Technology will best position us to continue our momentum to deliver for our clients and colleagues," according to a memo seen by Business Insider.

JPMorgan also announced in the memo that Gerard Francis, formerly the chief product officer of data and AI, is leaving the firm. In February, the bank's head of AI research, Manuela Veloso, left after eight years.

The bank, with its nearly $20 billion technology budget, has been especially bullish on AI. CEO Jamie Dimon said on a recent earnings call that there are already more than 1,000 use cases for AI, and Business Insider previously reported that JPMorgan can track individual engineers' token usage.

With Heitsenrether leaving, here's who is directing the bank's AI strategy and rollout as it aims to remain a tech leader on Wall Street.

Lori Beer

As the global chief information officer, Lori Beer sits at the top of the firm's technology leadership, overseeing all the systems and infrastructure. She's a member of the operating committee and manages the bank's sprawling tech budget and nearly 65,000 technologists. Beer joined JPMorgan in 2014.

Scot Baldry

Scot Baldry already had a big job as JPMorgan's Chief Technology Officer, and is taking on even more responsibility as the Chief Data and Analytics Officer now that Heitsenrether has announced her retirement. In that role, Baldry will helm the bank's overall AI program and strategy.

Baldry joined JPMorgan in London in 2022, after stints at Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse, and T. Rowe Price, and reports to Beer. According to an internal memo announcing his expanded remit, Baldry will continue working with technology leaders across business lines to make sure the firm's AI strategy remains consistent.

The memo said his team will "focus on AI & data strategy and governance, commercialization and value delivery, and external engagement with policymakers, regulators and the broader ecosystem."

Manoj Sindhwani

As part of the recent shakeup, Manoj Sindhwani, who was already the chief information officer for AI/ML and data platforms, is also taking responsibility for the bank's data and AI product team. He now oversees the employees who design and build firmwide data platforms and execute the broad strategy. Sindhwani has been at JPMorgan since 2024, after nearly a decade at Amazon, and reports to Beer.

William Patrick Opet

William Patrick Opet oversees all of JPMorgan's information security, technology controls, and risk management, which have become increasingly pressing issues in the age of AI. As part of his job, Opet ensures that the bank's AI systems are secure and appropriately controlled, and that the firm is protected against cyber threats, including those enabled by AI.

Opet joined JPMorgan in 2014 after working at Lockheed Martin and has been in his current role since 2021. He reports to Beer.

Mark Birkhead

As the firmwide chief data officer, Mark Birkhead's role has only become more crucial as AI has gotten more advanced. JPMorgan has more than an exabyte, or one billion gigabytes, of data across the firm, and Birkhead is the man who ensures it's AI-ready for both LLMs and generative AI.

Birkhead, who joined JPMorgan in 2020 and now reports to Baldry, said in a recent post on LinkedIn that "data strategy is the competitive differentiator in banking."

Arvind Joshi

Arvind Joshi manages JPMorgan's almost $20 billion annual technology budget, including its investments in AI. He oversees resource allocation and has recently commented on the importance of managing the ballooning price of AI tokens on LinkedIn. Joshi has been at JPMorgan for more than two decades and reports to Beer.

Sumitra Ganesh

Sumitra Ganesh took over as the head of AI research at JPMorgan in February, the latest position in her decade-long run at the bank. Veloso, who left in February, started the research team in 2018, and told Business Insider in 2021 that it focuses on big, "what-if" questions. As of April, JPMorgan had the largest AI research team among the 50 banks that the intelligence platform Evident AI tracks. Ganesh's research has primarily focused on multi-agent systems in finance, according to her LinkedIn.

items.title: How to Store Petabytes of Data Without Renting It From the Cloud
items.summary: Store one petabyte on Azure’s hot tier for five years and the bill runs close to $1.2 million, before you’ve moved a single byte back out. Try to retrieve that data and the cloud charges again: AWS bills roughly $90,000 in egress fees to pull a single petabyte off its platform, and Google Cloud Storage charges even more per gigabyte on the way out than AWS does. At ten, fifty, or five hundred petabytes, that arithmetic stops being a line item and starts being a strategic decision. This guide covers the real options for storing petabyte-scale data outside a public cloud provider: what they cost, what they require, and which companies have already proven the model works. Why the Cloud Gets Expensive at Scale, Specifically Cloud storage pricing is built around a simple asymmetry: getting data in is cheap or free, and getting data out is not. AWS charges $0.09 per gigabyte for the first 10 terabytes of egress, Azure charges around $0.087/GB, and Google Cloud Storage charges roughly $0.12/GB. Cloud providers generally charge four to six times more to retrieve data than to store it, which means the sticker price on a pricing calculator rarely reflects what you’ll actually pay once your data starts moving, whether that’s backups, analytics pipelines, disaster recovery, or a full migration. This isn’t a fringe concern. According to Flexera’s State of the Cloud Report, the share of enterprise workloads that organizations have pulled back out of the public cloud rose from 21% in the 2025 report to roughly 23% in the 2026 edition. That’s a steady, incremental shift rather than a stampede, and cloud adoption overall is still growing faster than repatriation is shrinking it. But it confirms the pattern: companies aren’t abandoning the cloud, they’re rebalancing it, keeping unpredictable workloads there while moving steady, predictable storage onto infrastructure they control directly. Option One: Run Your Own Object Storage The most direct replacement for S3 or Azure Blob Storage is software that speaks the same API but runs on hardware you control. Cloudian HyperStore, Scality RING, MinIO, and Caringo Swarm all deliver S3-compatible object storage on ordinary x86 servers, which means applications built around the S3 API don’t need to be rewritten. Scality RING scales to hundreds of petabytes and billions of objects across commodity hardware, and MinIO ships as a binary under 100MB that runs anywhere from an edge server to a full data center. TrueNAS takes a different route, layering file, block, and object storage on ZFS for multi-petabyte deployments that need strong data integrity guarantees. The appeal here is straightforward: you pay once for the hardware and the software license (or nothing, in MinIO’s open-source case), and there’s no per-gigabyte toll on the way out. Durability comes from erasure coding rather than the triple replication cloud providers use internally, which keeps the physical footprint and the power bill lower than you’d expect for petabyte-scale clusters. Option Two: Colocation Instead of Construction Owning the hardware doesn’t mean building a data center. Colocation lets you install your own servers and storage arrays inside a third-party facility that handles power, cooling, physical security, and network connectivity. Your data stays on equipment only your organization controls, which matters for regulated industries where auditors want to see exactly who can physically touch a drive. For steady-state, predictable workloads, on-premises and colocation deliver comparable total costs, and colocation tends to win on flexibility since you’re not committing capital to a building. Cloud, by comparison, runs roughly 60% more over five years for equivalent steady-state capacity once storage, compute, and data movement are all counted. Colocation is the practical middle ground for companies that want to escape cloud storage economics without taking on facilities management. Option Three: Tape for the Data You Rarely Touch Most petabyte-scale data isn’t accessed daily. It’s compliance archives, media libraries, historical logs, and backups that need to exist somewhere durable and cheap, not somewhere fast. This is where LTO tape still wins by a wide margin. LTO-9 cartridges hold 18TB natively and cost around $90 each, which works out to roughly $5 per terabyte in raw media cost. Storing 100TB on Amazon S3 Standard for five years runs well over $130,000; the same 100TB on LTO-9 tape costs a few hundred dollars in cartridges once you own the drive. Tape isn’t a replacement for active storage, retrieval times are measured in minutes, not milliseconds, and it requires drives, libraries, and someone who knows how to manage a tape rotation. But for the cold portion of a petabyte-scale archive, which is usually the majority of it, tape remains the cheapest storage medium that exists. The Companies That Already Did This Dropbox proved the model at genuine scale. Between 2015 and 2016, the company moved 500 petabytes of customer data off AWS and onto its own infrastructure, a project it called Magic Pocket, custom-built storage boxes and all. According to figures in Dropbox’s 2018 IPO filing, the migration saved the company $74.6 million over two years: a $92.5 million drop in third-party data center spending, offset by a $53 million increase in its own infrastructure costs, with an additional $35.1 million saved in 2017. Dropbox still keeps a small fraction of workloads on AWS where it makes sense, which is the pattern worth noting: this was a rebalancing, not an ideological exit. 37signals offers a smaller, more recent case study. After DHH announced the company’s cloud exit in October 2022, 37signals spent roughly $700,000 on Dell hardware, recouped that investment within the year, and brought its annual cloud bill down from a $3.2 million run rate to $1.3 million by 2024. The company now projects total five-year savings north of $10 million, achieved without adding infrastructure staff. Neither company treated this as a one-time migration. Both built the operational capacity to run storage as a permanent function, which is the real commitment this decision requires. Building the Business Case Before committing capital, run the numbers the way these companies did. Audit your access patterns first: separate hot data (accessed constantly), warm data (accessed occasionally), and cold data (accessed rarely), since the right storage tier is different for each. Calculate a genuine five-year total cost of ownership for your current cloud footprint, including egress and retrieval charges, not just the monthly storage line. Choose an S3-compatible software layer if you go the on-premises or colocation route, so existing applications don’t need architectural surgery. And if you operate in a regulated industry, factor in data sovereignty requirements early: the question isn’t only where the data physically sits, but which jurisdiction’s laws govern it and who can be legally compelled to hand it over. Enforcement is real money at this point: independent trackers put cumulative GDPR fines at more than €7.1 billion since the regulation took effect in May 2018, with Ireland’s Data Protection Commission alone accounting for roughly €4.04 billion of that total. None of this argues that the cloud is finished. Most companies still belong there for compute elasticity and workloads that spike unpredictably. But at petabyte scale, storage stops behaving like a rented service and starts behaving like infrastructure, and infrastructure is almost always cheaper to own outright than to lease indefinitely. That same instinct, questioning what you’ve been told to accept by default, is starting to show up beyond infrastructure too. As AI assistants like ChatGPT and Perplexity increasingly answer questions that used to send traffic to a search results page, agencies such as Liplyn now help brands earn a place inside those AI-generated answers rather than leaving that visibility to chance. Dropbox and 37signals didn’t leave the cloud because it was fashionable. They left because someone finally ran the five-year math. Datafloq is part of Liplyn Information Group. items.title: Sam Altman says one of his biggest fears is that a small number of companies will control AI: 'That'd be very, very bad'
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sam Altman says one of his biggest fears is what he calls "AI authoritarianism." That's when AI is controlled by a small number of companies or countries that gatekeep the tech. A debate over AI access erupted last week after the release of Kimi K3, a Chinese open-source model. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says one of his biggest concerns about AI isn't whether it becomes too powerful in and of itself, but that a single company could control that power. "I think the fight of the current moment is: Are we going to head to a world of AI authoritarianism or liberty?" Altman said on the latest episode of the "Relentless" podcast. "Every time that humanity has traded off its liberty for safety, it's been a long-term net loss," Altman said. "We are going to put this in the hands of people. We're going to empower them. We are going to let society express its ideas and use this technology in the way they want." It's a striking argument from the head of OpenAI , one of a small number of companies that control the world's most powerful AI models. OpenAI is also proprietary rather than open-source, meaning it doesn't share its tech. Altman's comments are well-timed. They follow a debate that erupted in Silicon Valley and Washington last week over how much visibility the general public should have into the architecture of frontier models. The recent release of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a powerful Chinese open-source model , sparked calls from some US officials to restrict access to Chinese models — and warnings from investors and startup founders that doing so could weaken global competition. The divide extends beyond model access. US export controls already determine which countries and companies can obtain the most advanced chips and computing capacity, giving Washington significant influence over who can build cutting-edge AI. Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, and many other leading tech companies signed a letter urging Washington not to restrict open-source AI. Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor and arguably the leading AI company on the planet right now, was the only major frontier lab that neither signed the letter nor publicly supported its contents. The company is known for taking a more cautious approach — arguing that increasingly capable models require stronger safeguards and tighter controls. Altman, meanwhile, said preventing such power from becoming overly concentrated has long been central to his vision for AI, even as his company continues to keep its own models closed. "For so long now, I have felt focused on this singular goal of abundant intelligence and a belief that incredible human prosperity will come from that, as long as we don't have a weird power concentration and kind of a new authoritarianism," he said. items.title: Satya Nadella says trust in US technology will outweigh the allure of cheap Chinese models
items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. George Chan/Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says trust in America's tech will help keep Chinese competitors at bay. Nadella was asked on CNN about the rise of Chinese models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3. He said the US's competitive advantage lies in its robust ecosystem of model training, too. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says trust in US AI technology and its robust training ecosystem will keep it competitive against Chinese products. Nadella was speaking to CNN's Fareed Zakaria on an episode of "GPS on CNN" that aired on Sunday. Zakaria asked Nadella whether Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 — a model that upset US tech stocks — and Chinese technologies have an edge over American products, because they're "much cheaper" and can do what most companies need. Nadella responded that the US has taken an "ecosystem approach" to shore up the competitiveness of its digital sector. "It's been about trust in our technology, right? So, for example, if you take the Chinese models, guess where these models run? They run on a lot of the hyperscalers — that are American — all over the world," Nadella said. He added that because the Chinese models are open weight, US companies can monitor, test, and post-train them. "I think that one of the things that's lost in this is the understanding even of how the US became competitive in the first place," Nadella said. "We became competitive because we took our technology, we built a rich ecosystem where others could participate, in other countries, and trust our stewardship of this ecosystem," he added. "And as long as that remains, we will absolutely be competitive, and we will win." Microsoft has big stakes in the US AI game. The tech giant holds about 27% of OpenAI's for-profit public benefit corporation. American AI companies face fierce competition from Chinese rivals, some of which have released bombshell products that roiled tech stocks. Last year, the emergence of the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek prompted a $1 trillion tech sell-off, one of the first major signs that China could rival US AI capabilities at a much lower cost. In July, Moonshot AI's new AI model, Kimi K3, made waves in the tech sphere for its coding, reasoning, and knowledge work abilities, all of which could rival those of models from Anthropic and OpenAI. items.title: I took a 30% pay cut to move to Spain. I made budgeting mistakes when adjusting to my new salary, but it was worth it.
items.summary: Damien Monel says he made trade-offs to live the life he wanted. Damien Monel Damien Monel took a 30% pay cut at his Amazon job to transfer from Cork to Madrid. He started spending half his paycheck on rent and made some budgeting mistakes, but has no regrets. Monel has more than doubled his salary since moving to Madrid and says following his gut was the key. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Damien Monel, a 28-year-old recruiter based in Madrid. It's been edited for length and clarity. I moved from my home country, France, to Ireland at 19 for a technical support role at Apple, only to burn out in my second year. I was staying at home in bed in the dark, not seeing friends, and I thought, I'm too young to feel this depressed. I knew I wanted to get into recruiting, so I applied for job after job until I landed a multi-month contract role at Amazon, also in Ireland. It was a pay cut and a temporary role, but I told myself I'd take the risk because there was no way I'd keep letting burnout affect me. Two years later, after transitioning into a full-time recruiter role at Amazon, I felt like I'd stopped growing as a person in Ireland. I transferred to Amazon's Madrid office in 2022 without ever having been to Spain, knowing that if I'd moved before, I could do it again. I had a bit of a weird feeling when I discovered my salary would be 30% lower, but four years later, I've more than doubled that lower salary. Along the way, I made mistakes, drained my savings, and spent most of my income on rent, but it was all worth it. Now, I think I'm ready to close my Spanish chapter and move on to what's next. I took two pay cuts without a backup plan Technical support at Apple wasn't my dream job, but I assumed it would be a great way to get started in the corporate world. It turned out not to be the Irish life I hoped to experience. I wanted to work on my English and immerse myself in the culture. I worked alongside a team of French colleagues, receiving angry phone call after angry phone call from unhappy French customers. Damien Monel says he made trade-offs to live the life he wanted.

Damien Monel

  • Damien Monel took a 30% pay cut at his Amazon job to transfer from Cork to Madrid.
  • He started spending half his paycheck on rent and made some budgeting mistakes, but has no regrets.
  • Monel has more than doubled his salary since moving to Madrid and says following his gut was the key.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Damien Monel, a 28-year-old recruiter based in Madrid. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I moved from my home country, France, to Ireland at 19 for a technical support role at Apple, only to burn out in my second year. I was staying at home in bed in the dark, not seeing friends, and I thought, I'm too young to feel this depressed.

I knew I wanted to get into recruiting, so I applied for job after job until I landed a multi-month contract role at Amazon, also in Ireland. It was a pay cut and a temporary role, but I told myself I'd take the risk because there was no way I'd keep letting burnout affect me.

Two years later, after transitioning into a full-time recruiter role at Amazon, I felt like I'd stopped growing as a person in Ireland. I transferred to Amazon's Madrid office in 2022 without ever having been to Spain, knowing that if I'd moved before, I could do it again.

I had a bit of a weird feeling when I discovered my salary would be 30% lower, but four years later, I've more than doubled that lower salary. Along the way, I made mistakes, drained my savings, and spent most of my income on rent, but it was all worth it.

Now, I think I'm ready to close my Spanish chapter and move on to what's next.

I took two pay cuts without a backup plan

Technical support at Apple wasn't my dream job, but I assumed it would be a great way to get started in the corporate world. It turned out not to be the Irish life I hoped to experience. I wanted to work on my English and immerse myself in the culture.

I worked alongside a team of French colleagues, receiving angry phone call after angry phone call from unhappy French customers. It felt like I was still in France, and I didn't have many opportunities to improve my English.

Moving on to my role at Amazon was a step in the right direction, but I still felt limited. Cork, where I lived, is a very small town, and there was so much more I wanted to see.

I started learning Spanish through Duolingo, went on a two-month trip to Latin America, and loved it. The lifestyle seemed amazing, and I wanted to trade Cork's rain for some sun.

I asked my manager for a transfer to an Amazon office in Spain, and she offered a move to Madrid or Barcelona. I chose Madrid for its architecture, atmosphere, and overall lifestyle. I didn't care about the 30% pay cut. I had this feeling that I'd taken a risk before and could do it again.

I remember crying at the airport before moving from France to Ireland. It was the toughest decision I'd ever made, but it turned out to be the best of my life. My experience figuring it out in Cork gave me the strength to handle more uncertainty.

When I first moved to Spain, I spent half my paycheck on rent

I watched a lot of YouTube videos about the Spanish lifestyle and got in touch with colleagues living there who could explain the cultural differences and direct me to resources, like a housing website. They also told me about the actual differences in cost of living.

I've found groceries to be fairly comparable to Ireland, although some everyday things, such as coffee, wine, and going out for a drink, are noticeably more affordable.

I started paying more in rent to live alone in an apartment. I could've shared an apartment to cut costs, but I wanted an upgrade and a place I'd love and feel safe working from home in. I wasn't saving any money, but sometimes you need to make trade-offs to live the quality of life you want.

I don't have a plan B. I can't just go to my parents' house if I don't pay my rent because they don't live in the country. I only have myself, and I have to figure it out.

I made budgeting mistakes, but I'm happy I did

Poor budgeting put me in stupid situations, and I had months where I went completely over budget and was basically living on my credit card. It wasn't the best decision because I paid a lot in interest and brought my savings down to zero, but it was my choice. I'm happy I did because I've had a great experience living alone.

I've enjoyed the Spanish life as I wanted to live it. Looking back, I would've appreciated making smarter choices by spending and going out less, but I was young and wanted to get to know people. I messed up, but I'm happy I did.

Two years ago, I left Amazon for a higher-paying corporate job and also started a coaching business on the side. Since then, I've been in a much more stable financial situation. I figured it out exactly as I knew I would.

Your decisions don't have to make sense to the people around you

If I have a gut feeling that something feels right, even if it doesn't make much sense on paper, I try to trust it. People have told me I'm insane for moving or taking a pay cut, but my gut tells me what the right next step is.

I'm already planning my next move: I'll be in Dubai by the end of the year. The idea came up during a call with my manager, and I've set my mind on it.

We tend to overthink our decisions. A move, for example, is a big decision, but what is the cost of you — emotionally, physically, financially — staying in your current situation?

items.title: I racked up $40,000 in credit card debt and kept it a secret from everyone. At 40, I had to move in with my parents to pay it down.
items.summary: Johanna Dickson. Courtesy of Johanna Dickson Johanna Dickson moved back home to New Jersey to tackle $40,000 in credit card debt accumulated in NYC. Johanna's debt began with store credit cards and escalated due to financial mismanagement. She used a debt relief program to reduce her debt and plans to move to Washington state soon. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Johanna Dickson , a 42-year-old who moved back to her parents' house in New Jersey to help her pay off years of debt. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Living in New York City was always a dream of mine. I grew up 90 minutes away in New Jersey, but after graduating from college in 2006, I landed a job in marketing that paid enough to afford my first Manhattan apartment with roommates. I finally felt like I made it when I moved into my own studio apartment in Harlem in 2021. Over the 15 years I lived in NYC, I secretly incurred around $40,000 in credit card debt. In 2023, at age 40, I decided I needed to fix my finances. I moved back in with my parents and took a few other drastic measures to get back on my feet. Here's how I got into debt and what I've been doing to get out of it. My relationship with money was stable before I moved to NYC I grew up privileged in a two-parent home where both brought in income. My parents paid for college so that I didn't have to take out any loans. I got my first credit card from Victoria's Secret in 2009 so I could establish a line of credit. I tried to keep the balance low and pay it off quickly, and then it became impossible. I was also an authorized user on my mom's Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's cards, and I was offered the chance to open my own, which I naively did. What made it worse was that as I spent more, the credit card kept raising my spending limit. It made it easy to spend more and maintain a high balance. The balances became completely unmanageable. I accumulated $40,000 in debt Accruing that much credit card debt was awful and slightly embarrassing. I felt like I'd been given a real gift to not have student loan debt when I graduated from college. I threw it away by getting into credit card debt. A lot of the debt was from keeping up with the Joneses through shopping when I worked in a fashion-adjacent job. I felt like I needed to wear certain brands and trends to fit in. Making minimum payments never seemed like enough I wasn't trying to ignore my debt. I was always told that making minimum payments would help me pay off the debt faster. I was paying those, but because of the high interest, it felt like I wasn't making a dent. I work in publicity and have spent many years being underpaid. Even as my salary increased, my debt increased, because my bad shopping habits increased as well. Sometimes, if I got a bonus or a raise, I would reward myself by going shopping. I didn't have a savings account or an emergency fund I would look at my monthly bills and try to see how to spread my paycheck to cover all of it, plus my credit card minimum payments, and that's when I realized I didn't have very much money left over, and no savings. My dog was going through some health issues, and I racked up vet bills of over $700. It was so stressful trying to pull together enough money to pay that bill. I didn't have any leftover money for food until my next paycheck, a week later. It felt like I hit rock bottom. Moving back in with my parents was the only way I could afford to pay off my debt I never thought I'd move back home to my parents' house, but honestly, it was better than having random roommates. I was tired of hustling so hard to live in NYC, and I wanted to be serious about paying off my debt. I waited until my lease was up and moved in December 2023. I started making the 90-minute commute to work in the city two days a week and still earned my salary while saving about $2,500 on rent and utilities every month. I know it's a privilege to have parents who can create a safe place for you, as mine did, and I'm grateful for that. While my parents didn't ask me to pay for anything, I still tried to pitch in when I could and cover food and other expenses. I got rejected from a debt consolidation loan, but took another path One of my best friends mentioned that she got out of debt by taking out a debt consolidation loan , where a company lends you money to pay off your credit card debt, and you pay off the consolidated loan. I didn't qualify for any of them, but this was probably a blessing in disguise. Instead, they suggested a debt relief program where the company negotiates your debt with the credit card companies and reduces it. They were able to negotiate my debt down to $31,000, plus their fees of around $2,000. I've been paying $665 a month for the past five years I entered the program with six credit cards and have settled four of them completely. I'm planning to make my final payment in August. The hardest part of doing this was having to default on my credit card bills, which meant my credit score tanked . Every balance was sent to creditors, at which point my debt company could negotiate. This felt very strange. I only have two credit cards now As tempting as some store credit card offers are, I'll never open one again. I use my two credit cards to help me rebuild my credit score, but I use them sparingly, mostly for groceries or gas. If there's something I want to buy but I don't have the cash on hand, I'll use a buy-now, pay-later service instead. I did this to attend my cousin's wedding last year. I have a strict rule: I pay off the debt within the six installments and avoid the interest. I'm still a work in progress with my spending I'm an emotional shopper, and unfortunately, the last several years have not been great for my mental health. I use shopping as a distraction. I'm a work in progress, but I'm proud to have a game plan I follow every month. I create a list of all my bills, how much money I have left over after my paycheck, how much needs to go into savings, and how much I'm left with after that. I really try to stick to that. If I overspend my budget, I work really hard to make up the money. I'm planning to move out of my parents' house this year Spending this time at home has helped me bulk up my savings and stay on track with my debt payments. I'm worried about finding an apartment, but I'm hopeful because my credit score is slowly rising. I'm planning to move to Washington state this year for a change of scenery and also because the cost of living is much less than in NYC. I'll gain my independence back without sacrificing my finances. Be transparent about your debt and search for options that make sense for you I held onto my debt like it was a dirty secret, but when I decided to tell people about it, they helped point me in the right direction to get help. If you're not ready to tell people, research your options. I didn't know that debt restructuring programs existed until my friend mentioned it. My dad said that he's not proud of me for getting into debt, but he's proud of me for realizing the problem and figuring it out. It took longer than I hoped, but I'm almost at the finish line. items.summary_html:
Johanna Dickson.

Courtesy of Johanna Dickson

  • Johanna Dickson moved back home to New Jersey to tackle $40,000 in credit card debt accumulated in NYC.
  • Johanna's debt began with store credit cards and escalated due to financial mismanagement.
  • She used a debt relief program to reduce her debt and plans to move to Washington state soon.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Johanna Dickson, a 42-year-old who moved back to her parents' house in New Jersey to help her pay off years of debt. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Living in New York City was always a dream of mine. I grew up 90 minutes away in New Jersey, but after graduating from college in 2006, I landed a job in marketing that paid enough to afford my first Manhattan apartment with roommates. I finally felt like I made it when I moved into my own studio apartment in Harlem in 2021.

Over the 15 years I lived in NYC, I secretly incurred around $40,000 in credit card debt. In 2023, at age 40, I decided I needed to fix my finances. I moved back in with my parents and took a few other drastic measures to get back on my feet.

Here's how I got into debt and what I've been doing to get out of it.

My relationship with money was stable before I moved to NYC

I grew up privileged in a two-parent home where both brought in income. My parents paid for college so that I didn't have to take out any loans.

I got my first credit card from Victoria's Secret in 2009 so I could establish a line of credit. I tried to keep the balance low and pay it off quickly, and then it became impossible. I was also an authorized user on my mom's Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's cards, and I was offered the chance to open my own, which I naively did.

What made it worse was that as I spent more, the credit card kept raising my spending limit. It made it easy to spend more and maintain a high balance. The balances became completely unmanageable.

I accumulated $40,000 in debt

Accruing that much credit card debt was awful and slightly embarrassing. I felt like I'd been given a real gift to not have student loan debt when I graduated from college. I threw it away by getting into credit card debt.

A lot of the debt was from keeping up with the Joneses through shopping when I worked in a fashion-adjacent job. I felt like I needed to wear certain brands and trends to fit in.

Making minimum payments never seemed like enough

I wasn't trying to ignore my debt. I was always told that making minimum payments would help me pay off the debt faster. I was paying those, but because of the high interest, it felt like I wasn't making a dent.

I work in publicity and have spent many years being underpaid. Even as my salary increased, my debt increased, because my bad shopping habits increased as well. Sometimes, if I got a bonus or a raise, I would reward myself by going shopping.

I didn't have a savings account or an emergency fund

I would look at my monthly bills and try to see how to spread my paycheck to cover all of it, plus my credit card minimum payments, and that's when I realized I didn't have very much money left over, and no savings.

My dog was going through some health issues, and I racked up vet bills of over $700. It was so stressful trying to pull together enough money to pay that bill. I didn't have any leftover money for food until my next paycheck, a week later.

It felt like I hit rock bottom.

Moving back in with my parents was the only way I could afford to pay off my debt

I never thought I'd move back home to my parents' house, but honestly, it was better than having random roommates. I was tired of hustling so hard to live in NYC, and I wanted to be serious about paying off my debt.

I waited until my lease was up and moved in December 2023. I started making the 90-minute commute to work in the city two days a week and still earned my salary while saving about $2,500 on rent and utilities every month. I know it's a privilege to have parents who can create a safe place for you, as mine did, and I'm grateful for that.

While my parents didn't ask me to pay for anything, I still tried to pitch in when I could and cover food and other expenses.

I got rejected from a debt consolidation loan, but took another path

One of my best friends mentioned that she got out of debt by taking out a debt consolidation loan, where a company lends you money to pay off your credit card debt, and you pay off the consolidated loan. I didn't qualify for any of them, but this was probably a blessing in disguise.

Instead, they suggested a debt relief program where the company negotiates your debt with the credit card companies and reduces it. They were able to negotiate my debt down to $31,000, plus their fees of around $2,000.

I've been paying $665 a month for the past five years

I entered the program with six credit cards and have settled four of them completely. I'm planning to make my final payment in August.

The hardest part of doing this was having to default on my credit card bills, which meant my credit score tanked. Every balance was sent to creditors, at which point my debt company could negotiate. This felt very strange.

I only have two credit cards now

As tempting as some store credit card offers are, I'll never open one again. I use my two credit cards to help me rebuild my credit score, but I use them sparingly, mostly for groceries or gas.

If there's something I want to buy but I don't have the cash on hand, I'll use a buy-now, pay-later service instead. I did this to attend my cousin's wedding last year. I have a strict rule: I pay off the debt within the six installments and avoid the interest.

I'm still a work in progress with my spending

I'm an emotional shopper, and unfortunately, the last several years have not been great for my mental health. I use shopping as a distraction. I'm a work in progress, but I'm proud to have a game plan I follow every month.

I create a list of all my bills, how much money I have left over after my paycheck, how much needs to go into savings, and how much I'm left with after that. I really try to stick to that. If I overspend my budget, I work really hard to make up the money.

I'm planning to move out of my parents' house this year

Spending this time at home has helped me bulk up my savings and stay on track with my debt payments. I'm worried about finding an apartment, but I'm hopeful because my credit score is slowly rising.

I'm planning to move to Washington state this year for a change of scenery and also because the cost of living is much less than in NYC. I'll gain my independence back without sacrificing my finances.

Be transparent about your debt and search for options that make sense for you

I held onto my debt like it was a dirty secret, but when I decided to tell people about it, they helped point me in the right direction to get help. If you're not ready to tell people, research your options. I didn't know that debt restructuring programs existed until my friend mentioned it.

My dad said that he's not proud of me for getting into debt, but he's proud of me for realizing the problem and figuring it out. It took longer than I hoped, but I'm almost at the finish line.

items.title: Actors are losing roles to AI knockoffs of themselves
items.summary: Brittany Marsicek was surprised to see a vertical drama she starred in remade with a character who acted and sounded like her. MoboReels Actors say AI micro dramas are using their likenesses and voices without their consent. The fast-growing mobile entertainment sector has rapidly embraced AI. The actors say they have little ability to fight back or get compensation. What does it feel like when an AI version of you takes your job? That was the strange reality facing actor Ashley BeLoat when she came across an AI-generated remake of a series she had starred in. Last year, BeLoat played the lead in "Hate the Way I Love You," a " micro drama " released by the app MoboReels, about a young couple whose future is shattered by a cancer diagnosis. She was shocked to discover, a few months later, that a series with the same plot appeared on the same app. The AI-generated actor in her role appeared younger and glammed up — with longer hair and a plunging neckline — but mimicked BeLoat's movements and had a voice that sounded eerily like hers. A micro drama starring Ashley BeLoat, left, was remade with a younger-looking AI character. MoboReels BeLoat told Business Insider it felt like an affront to the personal experience she'd drawn on for the role, as a nurse who has worked in oncology and faced cancer in her personal life. "Being an actor is a very vulnerable thing," she said. "It requires us to live private moments in public." "If there's a lack of trust in who we're working for, not only does it prevent us from giving something good for the viewer, but it takes away the reason that we do this," she continued. BeLoat said that, through her manager, she'd been reaching out to the app, hoping to have the AI version of the show removed or get compensation. So far, she hasn't gotten a response. Ashley BeLoat was shocked to see her voice and movements replicated by an AI character. Stephanie Girard BeLoat's experience isn't an isolated incident in the $1.4 billion US micro drama industry, which has rapidly embraced AI. Several other actors and producers said their on-screen work had been remixed into AI versions without their knowledge or consent. It's part of a wider trend of AI roiling various aspects of the industry. Business Insider previously reported that some micro drama apps had switched productions to synthetic actors after originally casting humans, and had used AI to make misleading, sexualized promos as they fought to attract new viewers. These short-form series designed for mobile viewing — also called verticals — had been a rare bright spot for actors amid a yearslong slump in film and TV production. Now, those actors have to consider whether their own work helped fuel their potential AI replacements. The actors feel there's little they can do. Brittany Marsicek also starred in a MoboReels show — "Ex-Husband, Step Aside, Lady Boss Returns" — that was remade with AI. Her character looked different, but acted and sounded like her. Marsicek, who's acted in more than 25 verticals, said she didn't have any AI protections in her contracts and that, in general, they grant the producer broad editing permissions. These jobs are often nonunion and feature early-career actors, who worry about the risks of speaking out. Brittany Marsicek starred in a series that was remade with an AI character that acted and sounded like her. Stephanie Girard "You're thinking, OK, maybe they'll edit it to be horizontal instead of vertical," Marsicek said of the contract. "You don't think that their editing includes completely changing your likeness." Actors say they've also felt the impact of AI in the number of auditions and jobs they've been able to get. BeLoat had been acting full time in verticals, but has since returned to nursing work. It's a sign of what could come for prestige Hollywood, as AI increasingly creeps into TV and film and studios look to cut spending. Right now, Hollywood studios have leeway to use AI, though they're constrained by restrictions and the potential for blowback from audiences and A-listers. Under their 2026 contract with the actors' union, SAG-AFTRA, studios can make AI-generated avatars that don't look like a particular person if they bargain with the union, said Jonathan Handel, an entertainment attorney. They can also create a digital replica of an actor's voice or likeness with the actor's consent. "This is the canary in the coal mine, and the reputational guardrail is something that over time might well erode as something becomes accepted in the micro drama world," Handel said. "That would put pressure on Hollywood, as well, to meet the economic change." Evan Gambardella said he felt "betrayed" when he recognized himself in an AI series, right, that he had no involvement in. GoodShort 'I felt dirty' Evan Gambardella starred in "Straight Until He Kissed Me," a "boys' love" drama about a med student and a CEO, released on GoodShort in September. While scrolling through the app recently, he said he recognized his face in a show called "Mafia King's Contract Groom," where the hero ends up marrying a crime boss. Gambardella said he felt "dirty and betrayed." He said he was grateful to GoodShort for helping him launch his acting career and to be part of a series that spoke to queer audiences. He felt he should have been informed and compensated for the use of his face, though. "I only got paid $5,000, but a lot of queer people saw themselves in it," he said. "When that show came out, I was heartbroken." Gambardella said he didn't think his contract had strong AI protections and couldn't prove the AI character was based on him, so he didn't see any point in fighting. For now, he's focusing on finding work with micro drama companies that are still casting real people. He added that since speaking out about his experience on social media, he hadn't gotten any work and felt that he may have been blacklisted. A rep for GoodShort said the app acquired "Mafia King's Contract Groom" from a third-party creator. The rep said GoodShort doesn't support the unauthorized use of an actor's image, voice, or identity, and that it's working with its partners to uphold standards that "respect performers, protect creative integrity, and provide audiences with transparency around how AI is used." Some actors have taken their complaints to social media to educate fans and urge them not to watch AI versions of themselves, lest it help those films' viewership numbers and validate the practice. Gambardella said he'd gotten comments from fans who thought his AI doppelganger was him. As AI videos get more realistic, it may get harder to tell what's real and what's not. "A lot of people thought I was AI," he said. Evan Gambardella believes he may have been blacklisted after speaking out on social media. Oliver Göttfert One of the biggest players in the micro drama space is testing the waters with AI. ReelShort's "Poolboy" was an early queer-themed hit when it was released last year. Cast members and viewers spoke out on social media after ReelShort released an anime version titled "Under the Surface" with an identical plot and description. "The idea of AI taking jobs away from artists and big companies using AI to exploit creatives for profit — that idea is no longer an idea," said Jen Parkhill, the director of the original "Poolboy." "It's a real true circumstance that's arriving on our shores now — we need to be talking about profit sharing and artists having ownership over their IP." Some actors believe the AI films won't have staying power. Marsicek isn't so sure. "Even if half of the people cancel their subscriptions and don't watch verticals anymore, if there's still some people watching it, they're still making money because they're so much cheaper to make," she said.
